failure_modes: Co-eluting non-vesicular particles (lipoproteins, protein aggregates, or matrix complexes) bind capture reagents and co-localize with particle peaks while being detergent/protease-resistant under the assay conditions, causing false-positive EV identity calls.

Spike-in tracer is not compositionally or biophysicaly representative of endogenous EVs (different density, surface ligands, or detergent sensitivity), so spike-in recovery validates assay mechanics but does not validate that endogenous captured material is membrane-protected EVs (false reassurance).

Capture-reagent cross-reactivity or nonspecific binding to abundant secretome components produces endogenous signal that mimics EV-marker capture despite absence of intact EVs (misleading identity readout).

Buffer or fractionation incompatibility with capture reagents or particle counters causes selective loss or masking of endogenous signals (false negatives) while spike-in (if optimized differently) remains recoverable, leading to inconsistent or misleading within-lot comparisons.

Detergent/protease conditions chosen to preserve spike-in readout may be insufficient to disrupt certain non-vesicular particles or conversely too harsh and destroy native EV epitopes, producing discordant spike-in versus endogenous protection behaviors and making the binary gate unmeasurable or uninterpretable.

Lot-to-lot biological variability in EV abundance or composition causes true absence of endogenous capture-positive, detergent-sensitive signal in some lots despite valid fractionation; this is indistinguishable from analytical failure without orthogonal compositional assays, causing inappropriate rejection or unnecessary rework.

Analytical sensitivity limits in particle counting or immuno-detection (especially for low-yield conditioned medium) result in failure to observe co-localization even when intact EVs are present, producing false negatives and undermining reproducibility across the >=3-lot requirement.

Labeling or tracer readout artifacts (bleaching, dissociation, species overlap) reduce spike-in detectability in some fractions, yielding inconsistent spike-in recovery that prevents assay-controlled discrimination (method failure).

Species- and route-dependent in vivo detectability (e.g., intranasal delivery) is poorly predicted by the in vitro identity gate—an EV-enriched pass may not translate to biological exposure or function in larger species, thus misleading downstream advancement decisions.
strongest_objection: The single strongest bounded failure mode is that endogenous capture-positive signal that co-localizes with particle-count peaks will frequently reflect detergent-resistant, non-vesicular co-isolates (lipoproteins, protein aggregates, matrix complexes, or labeled debris) or capture-reagent cross-reactivity rather than bona fide membrane-enclosed EVs; because such species can co-fractionate with particle peaks and survive the chosen detergent/protease conditions (or require harsher disruption that also destroys spike-in readout), the proposed spike-in–controlled qualitative gate can systematically misclassify secretome-like lots as ‘EV-enriched’ or produce unresolvable ambiguous calls despite validated spike-in recovery.
